title: The compactification category is nonempty, cofiltered, and base-changes
statement:
Let $S$ be a quasi-compact, quasi-separated scheme and let $f\colon X\to S$
be separated and of finite type. Let $\operatorname{Comp}(f)$ be the
category whose objects are the compactifications
$c=(X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{\bar f}S)$ of $f$ in the sense of
[def-nagata-compactification] ($j$ a quasi-compact open immersion, $\bar f$
proper, $\bar f\circ j=f$; scheme-theoretic density of $j$ is *not*
required), and whose morphisms $u\colon c_1\to c_2$, the *refinements*, are
the proper $S$-morphisms $u\colon\overline X_1\to\overline X_2$ with
$u\circ j_1=j_2$. Then:

1. $\operatorname{Comp}(f)$ is nonempty.
1. **(i)** Any two objects $c_1,c_2$ admit a common refinement
$c\to c_1$, $c\to c_2$; hence every finite family of objects admits one.
One such $c$ is the scheme-theoretic image $\overline X$ of
$(j_1,j_2)\colon X\to\overline X_1\times_S\overline X_2$, and for it
$j$ is scheme-theoretically dense.
1. **(ii)** Any two parallel refinements $u,v\colon c_1\to c_2$ are
equalized by a further refinement $c'\to c_1$.

In particular $\operatorname{Comp}(f)$ is cofiltered. Moreover it is
compatible with base change: let $g\colon S'\to S$ be any morphism and
$f'\colon X'=X\times_SS'\to S'$ the base change of $f$.

1. For every object $c$ of $\operatorname{Comp}(f)$, its base change
$c_{S'}=(X'\xrightarrow{j'}\overline X\times_SS'\to S')$ is an object of
$\operatorname{Comp}(f')$, and for every refinement $u\colon c_1\to c_2$ the
base change $u'=u\times_SS'$ is a refinement $c_{1,S'}\to c_{2,S'}$,
functorially in $u$. Consequently base change carries a common refinement
$c\to c_1,\ c\to c_2$ to a common refinement
$c_{S'}\to c_{1,S'},\ c_{S'}\to c_{2,S'}$, and equalizing refinements to
equalizing refinements.
1. If $c$ is the common refinement constructed in (i) from $c_1,c_2$ and
$c'$ the one constructed from $c_{1,S'},c_{2,S'}$, then the ambient scheme
of $c'$ is a closed subscheme of that of $c_{S'}$, and the inclusion is a
refinement $c'\to c_{S'}$ over the two projections. If $g$ is flat, this
inclusion is an isomorphism, i.e. the construction of (i) commutes with
flat base change.

Scheme-theoretic density is not preserved by arbitrary base change, which
is why it is not part of the objects: $c_{S'}$ need not be
scheme-theoretically dense ([def-nagata-dense-compactification]) even if
$c$ is, but it always is when $g$ is flat.

Here, for the quasi-compact morphisms whose images occur above, the scheme-theoretic image means the smallest closed subscheme through which the morphism factors, equivalently the closed subscheme cut out by the kernel of the structural map on sheaves.

proof.text: Identities are proper: the identity is a closed immersion, hence proper. Proper maps compose by the cited composition lemma. The identities and composites preserve the equations over S and on X, by associativity. The category laws are inherited from scheme morphisms. A map over S between two ambient schemes is proper by the proper-to-separated-target lemma: the source is proper over S and the target is separated because it is proper. Thus these are exactly the stated refinements.

Nagata applies because S is quasi-compact and quasi-separated and f is separated of finite type. Its compactification is an object of Comp(f), with the quasi-compact open immersion and proper structure map specified by the definition. This proves nonemptiness, including when X is empty.

For objects c_1,c_2 put Y=bar X_1 times_S bar X_2 and a=(j_1,j_2):X→Y. The projection Y→bar X_1 is a base change of the proper map bar X_2→S, so Y→S is proper by composition, and hence separated. The graph X→X times_S bar X_2 is a closed immersion: it is the pullback of the closed diagonal of bar X_2→S along (j_2 pr_X,pr_2). The second map X times_S bar X_2→Y is the base change of j_1, so is an open immersion. Thus a is a closed immersion followed by an open immersion, which is exactly an immersion. Moreover a is of finite type by the finite-type-to-separated-target lemma applied to X→Y→S; in particular a is quasi-compact. These arguments check every hypothesis needed for the image construction.

source.place: Proof: (i), graph and proper fibre product

proof.text: Apply the immersion compactification construction to a and the proper map Y→S. The cited immersion theorem makes C(a) a compactification, whose ambient scheme is SIm(a), and the image-factor theorem makes its open immersion j quasi-compact and scheme-theoretically dense. The restricted projections p_i:SIm(a)→bar X_i are over S and satisfy p_i j=j_i by the image factorization equality. They are proper by the proper-to-separated-target lemma since the source is proper over S and each target is separated over S. They are the required refinements. In Lean reuse the already proved graph-image construction Compactification.inf: inf_Z identifies its ambient scheme, isSchemeTheoreticallyDominant_inf_i gives density, and infFst and infSnd give the two refinements. This keeps the graph-image construction of the unit.

For the empty finite family choose the object from nonemptiness; a singleton refines itself by its identity. Inductively refine an object already refining the first n objects together with object n+1 by the pair construction. Compose its arrows to the previous objects. Associativity preserves their required equations, and properness of composites was checked in step 1. This proves the finite-family assertion. The Lean finite-family assertion uses IsCofiltered.inf_objs_exists on the finite image of the family; this library lemma is exactly the finite induction described here.

For parallel u,v:c_1→c_2 let E be the pullback of the diagonal of bar X_2→S along (u,v):bar X_1→bar X_2 times_S bar X_2. The target structure map is separated, so its diagonal is closed; closed immersions base-change, hence i:E→bar X_1 is closed. Consequently E→S is proper. The equality u j_1=v j_1 gives a unique j_E:X→E with i j_E=j_1 by the pullback universal property. Since i is a monomorphism, the square with upper map id_X, left j_E, right j_1 and bottom i is cartesian: for t:T→X and e:T→E with j_1 t=i e, cancellation in i j_E t=i e forces e=j_E t. Thus j_E is the base change of j_1, so is open. The open-immersion-quasi-compactness lemma applies to X→E→S, since f is finite type and E→S is proper, hence separated. Therefore j_E is quasi-compact. The pair (j_E,E→S) is a compactification; i is a proper refinement and equalizes u and v. Monomorphism cancellation here is elementary from the closed-subscheme description: a map factoring through a quotient sheaf has at most one such factorization. In Lean take a = pullback.lift r.hom s.hom and E = pullback a (pullback.diagonal d.g). Its first projection k is closed. The lift j is open because IsPullback.of_horiz_isIso_mono gives the cartesian square from j ≫ k = c.i. Give E the structure morphism k ≫ c.g and compare both projections of the pullback condition to prove that its refinement equalizes r and s.

A category is cofiltered precisely when it is nonempty, each pair of objects receives arrows from one object, and each pair of parallel arrows is equalized by an arrow into their source. Steps 2, 4 and 6 give these three properties. This is a direct application of that definition, without any smallness requirement on the collection of compactifications. The cofilteredness clause itself reuses the source library instance Compactification.isCofiltered under Nagata nonemptiness.

For any g:S′→S the cited base-change construction and theorem give a compactification c_S′ of f′. A refinement u base-changes to the induced map u′ of ambient fibre products. It is proper by proper base change. Its equations over S′ and on X′ follow by comparing both projections and applying the uniqueness in the fibre-product universal property. The same uniqueness proves (u w)′=u′ w′ and id′=id, so this is a functor. Applying these equalities to the two arrows of a common refinement and to u w=v w proves preservation of common and equalizing refinements. S′ need not be quasi-compact or quasi-separated: this step applies to a supplied compactification, not to Nagata on S′.

Let Z=SIm(a), Y=bar X_1 times_S bar X_2, Y′=Y times_S S′, and Z′=Z times_Y Y′. Fibre-product uniqueness identifies Y′ with bar X_1′ times_S′ bar X_2′ and the base change a′ with (j_1′,j_2′). It also identifies Z′ with the ambient scheme of c_S′. Since Z→Y is closed, Z′→Y′ is closed by closed-immersion base change, and a′ factors through it by j′. The image universal property gives a closed immersion k:SIm(a′)→Z′ compatible with Y′. This map also commutes with the maps from X′: composing the two candidate maps with the monomorphism Z′→Y′ gives a′, so they coincide. The closed immersion k is proper, hence a refinement; composing with either projection to bar X_i′ gives the required equality over the two projections. The construction of step 3 still applies over S′: it uses only the supplied proper ambient schemes, the finite type of f′, and open immersions, not qcqs of the base.

source.place: Proof: Base change, second part, comparison immersion

proof.text: Assume g flat. The projection Z′→Z is flat by flat base change. The map j:X→Z is quasi-compact and scheme-theoretically dense by step 4; it is quasi-separated because an open immersion is a monomorphism and its diagonal is an isomorphism, hence quasi-compact. The dense-flat-pullback lemma applied to j and Z′→Z says the scheme-theoretic image of j′:X′→Z′ is Z′. The open immersion j′ is quasi-compact because step 8 gives a compactification; thus the kernel description of the image specified in the statement says ker(O_Z′→j′_*O_X′)=0. This is precisely scheme-theoretic density. The closed immersion k of step 9 must therefore be an isomorphism. Indeed on an affine open Spec A of Z′ its source is Spec(A/I); every element of I vanishes after pullback along j′ because j′ factors through k. Injectivity of O_Z′→j′_*O_X′ forces I=0. Thus every affine restriction of k is the identity closed subscheme, proving the assertion. This uses the density clause actually stated by the cited node, not the stronger image-base-change assertion buried in its proof.

source.place: Proof: Base change, second part, flat comparison

proof.text: For the counterexample choose K = ULift of the rational field, R = K[t], S = Spec R, and U = D(t). The basic open is affine, so its inclusion is quasi-compact. The zero prime lies in U, since t is nonzero. The spectrum of the domain R is irreducible, hence U is topologically dense; since S is reduced, IsSchemeTheoreticallyDominant.of_isDominant makes its inclusion scheme-theoretically dominant. Let p be the prime kernel of evaluation at zero. Then p is outside U. Set T = Spec kappa(p) and let t0 : T -> S be the canonical residue-field morphism, whose value at every point is p. Compactify U -> S by S itself, using the identity proper structure map. All finiteness, separatedness, and qcqs hypotheses follow from affineness and the quasi-compact open immersion. If the base-changed open immersion were scheme-theoretically dominant, its quasi-compactness would imply topological dominance. The base-changed ambient structure map is an isomorphism because it is the base change of the identity. Therefore U times_S T -> T would be dominant. The spectrum of a field is nonempty, so dominance would give a point z of U times_S T. The pullback equation makes the image of its U-projection equal p, contradicting p not in U. This proves failure of density without a tensor-product computation. For flat base change and any c, derive QuasiCompact c.i from QuasiCompact f and apply the already proved isSchemeTheoreticallyDominant_i_baseChange; it is the dense-flat-pullback argument of step 10.
